picked.t: Vietnam gains market share as China’s 3rd biggest vegetable, fruit supplier
picked.body: China spent approximately US$2.16 billion importing vegetables, flowers, roots, and fruits from Vietnam, up 19.3% from the same period in 2025, according to data from China Customs. Vietnam’s share rose from 13.8% of China’s imports in the first half of 2025 to almost 16% to rank behind Thailand (37%) and Chile (17%). Vietnam’s rise has been driven by both scale and changes in its product mix, with durian emerging as the biggest growth driver. This year, China has paid nearly $988 million for imports of fresh and frozen durian from Vietnam, up 43% from the same period a year earlier.thos Shipments of coconut also rose sharply but of mango, dragon fruit, and banana declined. Dang Phuc Nguyen, secretary-general of the Vietnam Fruit and Vegetable Association, said the proximity allows fresh products from Vietnam to reach China quickly, maintain better quality, and incur lower logistics costs than exports from Southeast Asia and South America. This advantage is particularly important for fresh fruits, which are highly dependent on transportation time. As demand for tropical fruits in China expands from major cities to second- and third-tier cities and provinces in the country’s northern and western regions, suppliers located closer to China have greater room for growth. China’s approval for a growing number of Vietnamese fruits has enabled businesses to expand their growing areas and output. But China is also imposing increasingly stringent requirements on imports. Nguyen said China is tightening oversight across areas ranging from business registration and growing-area codes to packing facilities. Origin fraud, the misuse of growing-area codes, and pest contamination can result in codes being temporarily suspended or revoked, directly affecting the exports of an entire growing region, he said.

picked.t: Vietnamese fruit gains stronger foothold in global markets
picked.body: Held at AsiaWorld-Expo in Hong Kong on Sept. 2–4, the event features 730 exhibitors from 40 countries and territories. The Vietnamese delegation, organized by the Vietnam Fruit and Vegetable Association, comprises 24 booths representing 22 businesses nationwide. The trade fair serves as a platform connecting businesses, distributors and consumers, with products and services spanning fruit, machinery, logistics, smart agricultural solutions and technologies. Dang Phuc Nguyen, the associationa's secretary general, said the Vietnamese delegation has expanded steadily over the years, from 10 businesses in 2017 to 22 this year. At Asia Fruit Logistica 2025, Vietnamese firms signed contracts worth about US$5 million directly with international partners. Revenue is expected to be higher this year, driven by key products such as durian, passion fruit and dragon fruit. He noted that the scale and export value of Vietnam's participation remain modest compared to the country's huge fruit and vegetable potential. The event brings broader benefits by helping Vietnamese businesses find partners, expand markets and promote the quality and reputation of the country's fruit industry. According to Nguyen, the fair also features technologies for harvesting, processing, preservation and transportation, particularly smart, organic and environmentally friendly farming solutions. Vietnamese businesses can explore these technologies for potential imports or technology transfers to improve the quality and value of agricultural products. Le Minh Tuan, director of Pulimex Import-Export, said his company is displaying Vietnamese specialties including dragon fruit, coconut, banana, longan, rambutan and mango, mainly to seek partners and expand export markets. After four consecutive participations, he said he considered the Hong Kong fair an important platform for Vietnamese fruit exporters to reach markets not only in Asia but also in the U.S., Europe, Australia, the Middle East and Africa. He also appreciated stronger support from Vietnamese authorities in addressing legal procedures and payment-related difficulties. Le Huu Dung, director of Vinafood International, which exports Vietnamese fruits to India and the Middle East, expressed hope that the event will help the company expand into other potential markets, backed by the diversity and growing reputation of Vietnamese fruit. Alessandro Cordano from Portugal said he was impressed by the variety of Vietnamese fruits , describing them as attractive in appearance, delicious, and beneficial to health. Vietnam's fruit and vegetable exports have grown strongly in recent years, rising from about $7 billion in 2024 to $8.6 billion in 2025 and expected to surpass $10 billion this year.

picked.t: Russia, Philippines among fastest growing tourist markets for Vietnam
picked.body: The rise in Russian tourists has made Russia the largest European market and the third largest source of international arrivals to Vietnam this year, with around 1 million visitors, only after mainland China (3.5 million) and South Korea (2.8 million). Nguyen Tien Dat, CEO of AZA Travel, said: "Russian tourists enjoy swimming, sunbathing, eating seafood, and relaxing at resorts. Vietnam fully meets these needs, so it is understandable why they are visiting in large numbers," Dat says. Kristina Zagumennaya, director of a Russian travel agency, told the Russian news agency Sputnik in early August that Russian tourist flows are shifting between markets. While Turkey remains the top choice, Vietnam and China have recorded outstanding growth. "Vietnam stands out as a popular choice this tourist season," Zagumennaya said, noting that multiple charter flights are operating to destinations across the country to meet demand for both beach holidays and cultural tourism. In addition to charter flights, Vietnam Airlines increased the frequency of its direct Hanoi-Moscow route from three to four flights per week starting in July. Ranking behind Russia, the Philippines also showed notable growth, despite not being a prominent source market for Vietnamese tourism prior to 2025. Filipino visitors have risen to nearly 470,000 this year, among the 10 largest group of foreign visitors to Vietnam. Bui Thanh Tu, marketing director of BestPrice Travel, attributes this rise to more convenient flight routes, especially from Manila and Cebu, competitive costs, and tourism products that differ from the island destinations familiar to Filipinos. He also cites the viral impact of TikTok and YouTube videos featuring Hanoi, Sa Pa, Da Nang, and Hoi An. However, he notes that the strong growth was partly due to a low base last year, and says Vietnam needs to continue expanding air routes and developing suitable tourism products to sustain growth over the long term. In terms of overall volume of visitors in the first eight months, Asia remains the dominant region. Mainland China, South Korea, and Taiwan contributed around 6.2 million arrivals, accounting for nearly 40% of all international visitors to Vietnam.

picked.t: Why some Vietnamese workers are afraid to leave the office on time
picked.body: Official hours at Uyen’s private company in HCMC end at 5:30 p.m., but the 32-year-old marketing employee says she now routinely stays until after 7:30 p.m. or waits for her manager to leave first. She used to go home on time until a performance review two years ago, when she received an A- rating and a bonus US$192 lower than those of several colleagues. Her department head told her points had been deducted for her "work attitude" because she did not stay late like others and was therefore seen as less enthusiastic. "I don’t know when leaving work on time started being seen as a lack of dedication," Uyen says. Van Vy, 29, an IT employee in Hanoi, had a similar experience after failing to secure a salary increase in 2025. Although his job performance was good, his supervisor said he did not appear to be putting in enough effort because he "stood up to leave at 5:30 p.m. every single day." Vy has since adjusted his routine, spending more time over coffee in the morning and deliberately pushing work into the afternoon so he can remain at the office until around 7 p.m. The issue has become a frequent topic of debate on social media. One video discussing employees who leave as soon as working hours end drew 4.3 million views, while another debate over whether leaving on time reflects low emotional intelligence attracted nearly 270,000 viewers. Hundreds of posts have also appeared on Threads under the theme of being unable to leave work on time. Opinions are divided. Some argue that leaving on schedule after completing assigned tasks is professional, while others see an unwillingness to stay late as a sign of weak commitment. A VnExpress survey in August 2026 found that 13% of businesses assessed employees partly on the amount of time they spent in the office. Another poll of 2,000 readers found that 13% of workers finished their tasks on time but stayed behind because they feared being judged. This pressure to remain visible at work, even when productivity has dropped, is often described as presenteeism. A survey by U.K.-based health and wellbeing company Vitality found that presenteeism reduced productivity far more than absenteeism, costing an estimated 35 working days per employee each year. Still, some managers defend the practice. Thanh Toan, 45, director of an import-export company in Hai Phong, prefers employees to stay late because their physical presence can make coordination between departments easier and allow problems to be handled more quickly. He also believes voluntarily remaining after hours can signal responsibility, commitment and a willingness to put collective goals ahead of personal interests. Dr. Le Trung Hieu, deputy head of the human resource management department at the School of Business Administration, Vietnam National University, Hanoi, says Vietnam’s workplace culture has been shaped partly by its economic history and by increasing integration with East Asian business practices. "Foreign investment from East Asian countries have brought with it a work environment that emphasizes hierarchy, obedience to superiors, and consensus, along with fierce competitive pressure." Hieu adds that the reluctance to leave on time is also rooted in a widespread workplace assumption that longer hours reflect greater dedication. When companies lack clear performance indicators, managers may fall back on time spent at the office as a proxy for commitment, he says. From a psychological perspective, experts say some managers prefer to keep employees physically visible because it gives them a greater sense of control. Employees, meanwhile, may avoid leaving early because they fear conflict, being seen as less capable or losing promotion opportunities. Nguyen Thi Kieu Chinh, a financial adviser at FIDT Investment Consulting and Asset Management Joint Stock Company, says the phenomenon is particularly common in finance, technology and consulting in major cities, where daily output can be difficult to quantify. "Many people accept staying late because they fear appearing unmotivated or missing out on promotion opportunities," she says. But she warns that this kind of superficial display of commitment only offers short-term reassurance. Over time, it can erode motivation, increase staff turnover and drive away capable employees. It can also damage health and work-life balance. "A competitive economy is not built on the number of hours worked, but on the value generated during each hour," Chinh says. In Hanoi, sales manager Minh Phong, who oversees 20 employees, says he stopped judging staff by how late they stayed after realizing it did not improve performance. "I manage by deadlines for task completion, not by watching over adults like a preschool teacher," he says. Hieu recommends that businesses shift toward output-based management, establish transparent KPI systems and require employees to communicate progress clearly. picked.t: UK universities rush to cut tuition fees to win back international students amid decline
picked.body: At least 22 universities now provide automatic tuition-fee discounts to postgraduate taught students, with no separate application required, according to a review of 90 institutions by consultancy S Squared Insights, as cited by The Telegraph . Unlike traditional scholarships, students do not need to apply for or compete for these discounts. The reductions are automatically deducted from their tuition fees, with the amount varying by institution. Among them, the University of Aberdeen announced on its website it is granting international students a direct discount of up to £8,000, the largest reduction recorded so far. The University of Kent is offering a £5,000 tuition reduction for master’s programs to students from 14 countries and territories, including China, South Korea and Vietnam. The University of Nottingham, a member of the Russell Group of leading research universities in the U.K., is offering a £3,000 reduction. The Financial Times quoted Julian Westwood, director of S Squared Insights, as saying that universities had "shifted from smaller scholarship schemes to broad, overly simple cohort discounts." He warned that simultaneously facing declining student numbers and reduced per-student revenue could push some university financial plans beyond their stress-testing limits. Echoing these concerns, Zeenat Fayaz, founder of The Brand Education, told The Telegraph that this "pricing war" could backfire by forcing universities to compete on cost rather than educational strength. Fayaz noted that higher-tariff universities are also reducing grade requirements to admit more students, describing the escalating situation as "a race to the bottom." These discounts emerge as universities face intensifying competition to attract overseas applicants. International students pay higher fees than domestic students and provide a crucial source of revenue for the education sector. But their number has been going down. Latest Home Office data shows that applications for sponsored study visas fell by 11% to 381,500 in the year ending July 2026 , compared with the previous 12-month period. This decline in international recruitment largely follows the government's introduction of restrictions in January 2024, which prevent most overseas students from bringing family members to the U.K. There were 19,200 applications from student dependants in the year ending July 2026, a 6% drop from the previous year and a staggering 87% plunge compared with December 2023, before the restrictions took effect. According to the Office for Students (OfS), tuition fee revenue from postgraduate students stood at around £5 billion in the 2024-25 academic year, down £500 million from the previous year. In May, the Education Committee, a select committee of the U.K. House of Commons that checks and reviews the work of the Department for Education, warned that the government has no clear plan for universities facing insolvency. The committee warns that the U.K.'s higher education sector is under "unprecedented" financial pressure. These financial challenges are already having serious consequences, including staff redundancies, closures of courses and departments, recruitment freezes, and the selling off of assets. A total of 124 institutions, or 45% of the sector, could face budget deficits in the 2025-26 financial year without measures to mitigate the risks, compared with 96 providers that previously forecast a deficit in 2025-26. "Currently, there is no clearly understood protocol for how the government might respond to a situation of a provider at risk of imminent insolvency, which is a very serious problem," the committee said, as posted on the U.K. Parliament website. The U.K. had around 685,000 international students in the 2024-25 academic year. Average tuition fees for international master's students range from £15,000 to £45,000 per year, according to study-abroad consultancy ApplyBoard.

picked.t: Durian exports expected to hit $4B this year
picked.body: Dang Ngoc Diep, deputy minister of Agriculture and Environment, said at the government's regular press conference on Thursday that durian is one of the agricultural products with relatively high value, a cultivation area of about 200,000 hectares and an output of approximately 2.08 million tonnes. It is a key crop of the agriculture sector, accounting for about 40% of its total export turnover. In the first eight months, durian exports were estimated at $1.95 billion, of which exports to China alone accounted for $1.85 billion or 95%. In response to difficulties facing the fruit’s exports, the Ministry of Agriculture and Environment has sent working delegations led by deputy ministers to work directly with localities, particularly high-output growing areas in the Central Highlands, the southeastern and southwestern regions, and Dong Nai province, to remove bottlenecks, Diep said. On July 1, the ministry launched origin tracing through its electronic system. "We met with the trade counsellors of the US and China. They highly appreciated the ministry's implementation of origin tracing for the first time and its efforts to promote Vietnamese agricultural products as reputable brands domestically and internationally," Diep said, noting that this is one of the solutions to boost exports and increase the value of durian. The ministry has also worked to address difficulties and obstacles related to the issuance of growing-area codes. "All durian growing areas are now decentralised, allowing ward- and commune-level authorities to issue growing-area and packing-facility codes, making the process more convenient," he said. Following a meeting between ministry leaders and the Chinese side on Aug. 14, the General Administration of Customs of China granted 567 growing-area codes for Vietnamese durian, bringing the total number to more than 1,800. The deputy minister also pointed out several limitations in the durian sector, including rapid growth that has not yet been matched by the organization of value chains. In addition, technical and market requirements are becoming increasingly stringent. He also highlighted challenges from international competition, noting that countries such as Malaysia and Thailand have introduced policies to promote durian exports to China . Regarding measures to be implemented, the ministry will step up trade promotion and diversify export markets, including continuing negotiations to expand access and increase share in promising markets such as India, Australia and New Zealand. In July, India agreed to allow Vietnam to export durian to its market. This is a market of more than one billion people with very strong demand in the coming period. Works are underway to expand export promotion activities in India, he said. The second measure is to reorganize production and develop sustainable raw-material areas, while reviewing production-area planning to ensure compatibility with land, water resources, climate and infrastructure conditions. The third is to standardize quality, food safety and origin tracing while improving research, application and transfer of science and technology, as well as digital transformation. The two other measures are developing storage, processing and logistics infrastructure; and expanding and strengthening the capacity of the laboratory system.
